w:r.w:t: Detecting Lip-Sync Deepfakes Using Mouth-Closure Phoneme Analysis
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, School of Computer Science & Engineering
Galgotias University, Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh, India

Generative video synthesis has reached a point where a person's recorded speech can be re-timed to match new audio, producing what are commonly termed lip-sync deepfakes. A widely cited forensic countermeasure exploits a physical constraint of human articulation: producing the phonemes /m/, /b/, and /p/ requires the lips to close completely, a constraint many synthesis pipelines fail to reproduce with fidelity. This project investigates whether that detection cue continues to hold under conditions the original study did not test. The automatic classifier behind the technique was trained and validated on a single public figure, leaving its behaviour across speakers of different age, gender, and appearance unverified, and it was evaluated only against lip-sync generators from 2019 and 2020, a period that predates the diffusion-based and identity-aware synthesis methods now in common use. This work retrains the mouth-openness classifier on a multi-speaker corpus and re-evaluates its detection accuracy against generation methods released between 2024 and 2026. The outcome will indicate whether a lightweight, interpretable phonetic cue of this kind remains dependable at scale, a question that matters for content moderation, journalistic verification, and legal evidence review, settings where transparent and computationally inexpensive forensic tools are preferable to opaque, resource-heavy classifiers.
deepfake detection, lip-sync forgery, phoneme-viseme mismatch, multimedia forensics, generalization, video authentication

Video and audio synthesis tools have moved from a research curiosity to a practical fraud vector. In February 2024, a finance employee at a multinational firm authorized a transfer of twenty-five million dollars after a video call with what appeared to be the company's chief financial officer and other senior staff, all of whom were synthetic [3], [7]. Incidents of this kind, together with the routine use of face-swap and voice-cloning tools to manufacture fabricated political and celebrity statements, have made deepfake detection an active area of both academic research and applied digital forensics.

Detection approaches broadly split into two families. The first trains a classifier end-to-end on large collections of real and fake video, letting the network discover whatever statistical artifact separates the two classes; such models can be highly accurate on their training distribution but tend to behave as black boxes and degrade sharply on generators they have not seen [6]. The second family instead targets a specific, human-interpretable regularity that synthesis is expected to violate. Agarwal et al. [1] introduced one such cue for lip-sync deepfakes: producing the bilabial sounds /m/, /b/, and /p/ requires a speaker to close their lips fully, and many synthesized mouths fail to do so at the correct moment, creating a detectable phoneme-viseme mismatch. Because the cue is grounded in articulatory physiology rather than in whatever statistical fingerprint a particular generator happens to leave behind, it is comparatively lightweight, explainable, and inexpensive to compute — properties that matter for real-world deployment at the scale of a social media platform or a newsroom verification desk.

The original study, however, leaves two questions open. Its automatic mouth open/closed classifier was trained and validated using video of a single speaker, so nothing is known about how the classifier behaves on speakers of different age, gender, ethnicity, or facial structure. Separately, the technique was tested only against lip-sync generators available in 2019 and 2020; the field has since moved through several generations of GAN-based and diffusion-based talking-face synthesis [9]–[12], and it is not established whether the same articulatory failure the original detector relies on is still present in output from these newer systems.

This project addresses both questions together. We retrain the mouth-closure classifier on a multi-speaker, multi-ethnicity corpus so that its accuracy can be measured on speakers it has not seen during training, and we evaluate the retrained model against video produced by generation methods released between 2024 and 2026. Read together, the two experiments test whether the phoneme-viseme mismatch cue is a property of deepfake synthesis in general, or whether the original result was partly an artifact of a narrow speaker sample and an earlier generation of synthesis tools. The broader motivation aligns with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 16, which calls for accountable institutions and public access to reliable information; a lightweight forensic tool that needs no specialized hardware supports that goal at a scale heavier detection pipelines cannot easily match.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior work on deepfake generation, cue-based detection, and the generalization problem in this field. Section III restates the problem this project addresses. Section IV describes the proposed methodology, covering dataset construction, classifier retraining, and the modern generation methods used for evaluation. Section V outlines the planned experimental setup. Section VI discusses expected outcomes and their implications, and Section VII concludes with directions for future work.

Deepfake generation is commonly divided into face-swapping, face reenactment, talking-face (lip-sync) generation, and facial attribute editing [5]. This project is concerned with the third category, in which a source video's mouth region is regenerated to match a new audio track while the rest of the face and scene remain untouched. Early talking-face systems relied on convolutional generators trained with a lip-sync discriminator; more recent systems have moved toward diffusion-based architectures that condition generation on facial landmarks or audio-derived motion features to improve both image fidelity and temporal stability [9]–[11]. MoDiTalker [12], for example, separates audio-to-motion and motion-to-video generation into two diffusion modules specifically to address the temporal jitter that earlier GAN-based lip-sync methods exhibited around rapid mouth movements. These newer systems produce noticeably fewer visible per-frame artifacts than the generators available when the original phoneme-viseme detector was built, which is precisely why re-testing the underlying detection cue against them is necessary rather than assumed.
B. Cue-Based and Physiologically Grounded Detection

Agarwal et al. [1] proposed detecting lip-sync deepfakes by checking whether a speaker's mouth closes fully during bilabial phonemes, first through manual frame inspection and then through an automatic neural classifier trained on footage of Barack Obama's weekly addresses. Around the same period, Chugh et al. [2] proposed a related but distinct audio-visual cue, a modality dissonance score that measures synchrony between audio and visual streams more broadly rather than isolating a specific phoneme class. Both approaches share the appeal of the cue-based family described above: they target a mechanism of speech production rather than a generator-specific texture artifact, so in principle they should transfer across different synthesis methods.

More recently, Datta et al. [3] proposed PIA, a multimodal framework combining phoneme-temporal alignment with facial identity-dynamics embeddings, motivated by the observation that phoneme-viseme threshold checks alone are insufficient against modern generative models such as GANs, diffusion models, and neural rendering techniques. PIA is useful evidence for this project in two respects. First, it confirms that phoneme-level cues remain an active and credible line of forensic research five years after the original technique was published. Second, its framing implies, without directly testing, that the original single-cue detector may no longer be sufficient against current-generation synthesis on its own. This project tests that implication directly, rather than assuming it, by retraining and re-evaluating the original detector itself under modern conditions before concluding that additional multimodal signals are required.
C. Generalization Across Speakers and Generators

Generalization is widely reported as the central unresolved problem in deepfake detection. Croitoru et al. [6] benchmark a range of published detectors on out-of-distribution content and find that detectors calibrated on one set of generators consistently fail to generalize to deepfakes produced by generators absent from their training data. Nguyen-Le et al. [7] and Li et al. [8] reach a similar conclusion when surveying cross-dataset performance more broadly, attributing the drop to differences in feature distribution between training and test generators. The same concern applies to speaker diversity: a classifier calibrated on one individual's facial geometry and speaking style may key on properties specific to that person rather than on the phonetic regularity it is meant to detect. FakeAVCeleb [4], a multimodal dataset spanning four ethnic backgrounds with balanced gender representation, was built specifically to give audio-visual deepfake detectors a more diverse training and evaluation basis than earlier single-identity or narrow-demographic datasets provided. This project draws on the same design principle, applying it to the phoneme-viseme mismatch classifier rather than to a new detector architecture.

Table I summarizes how the present project relates to the two most directly relevant prior efforts. Agarwal et al. established the cue and validated it on a single speaker against early-generation deepfakes; Datta et al. extended the cue into a multimodal detector aimed at modern generators without re-validating the original single-cue method along either dimension. This project instead re-validates the original method along both the speaker and generator dimensions before any architectural extension is considered — a narrower but more direct test of whether the original cue's core assumption still holds.

The phoneme-viseme mismatch technique for lip-sync deepfake detection was trained and tested on video of a single speaker, so its ability to generalize to individuals of different age, gender, and facial appearance has not been established. The technique was also validated only against deepfake generation methods available between 2019 and 2020; whether the underlying detection cue — incorrect mouth closure during bilabial phonemes — still holds against substantially more advanced generation methods released between 2024 and 2026 is unknown. No published study has retrained and re-validated this method under both conditions at once, leaving a genuine gap in understanding whether a widely cited forensic technique remains practically useful today. This project addresses that gap by retraining the automatic mouth open/closed classifier on a diverse, multi-speaker dataset and by testing detection accuracy against video produced by current-generation deepfake tools, in order to determine whether the method's central assumption — that fake lip-sync video mismatches phoneme-to-viseme mapping — continues to hold true.

Fig. 1 outlines the overall pipeline. A video is first processed to isolate the speaker's mouth region and align it in time with a forced phonetic transcription of the accompanying audio; the mouth-closure classifier then scores each bilabial-phoneme interval as closed or not closed, and a video is flagged as manipulated when the rate of open-mouth bilabial frames exceeds a threshold calibrated on real video.

Where the original study relied on footage of a single speaker, this project builds a training and evaluation corpus spanning multiple speakers, genders, and ethnic backgrounds. Real video is sourced from existing multi-speaker corpora used elsewhere in the deepfake literature, such as VoxCeleb2 and LRS3, and paired with fake video drawn from FakeAVCeleb [4] as well as newly generated samples produced with the modern tools described in Section IV-C. Using an existing multi-identity corpus rather than collecting new footage keeps the dataset construction effort within the scope of a capstone project while still directly addressing the single-speaker limitation identified in Section III.

Each utterance is forced-aligned to its audio transcript to recover the start and end time of every phoneme, using an existing forced-alignment tool rather than manual annotation. Frames falling within an /m/, /b/, or /p/ interval are extracted and manually spot-checked on a sample of the real-video subset to confirm that full lip closure is in fact present, replicating the validation step used in the original study before automatic labeling is trusted at scale.
C. Mouth-Closure Classifier and Retraining Protocol

The classifier follows the same basic design as the original work — a convolutional network that takes a cropped mouth region as input and predicts whether the lips are closed — retrained from scratch on the multi-speaker corpus described above. Speakers are split by identity rather than by clip, so that no individual appearing in the training set also appears in the test set; this leave-speakers-out protocol is the step that actually measures cross-speaker generalization, rather than merely reporting accuracy on held-out clips of speakers the model has already seen.
D. Modern Deepfake Generation Methods for Evaluation

To test the second gap, evaluation video is generated using talking-face synthesis methods published between 2024 and 2026, including landmark-conditioned and motion-prior diffusion approaches [9], [10], [12] and a high-resolution diffusion-based lip-sync model [11]. These were chosen to span the architectural range now in common use — GAN-based, landmark-conditioned diffusion, and motion-disentangled diffusion — rather than testing against a single modern tool and generalizing from it.

Detection performance is reported using accuracy, precision, recall, and area under the ROC curve, computed separately for (i) held-out speakers evaluated against era-matched 2019–2020 generators, confirming the retrained model still performs comparably to the original on its own terms, and (ii) held-out speakers evaluated against the 2024–2026 generation methods, the condition central to this project's research question. Reporting both conditions separately is what allows any drop in accuracy to be attributed specifically to the generator era rather than to the retraining process itself.

The classifier and data pipeline are implemented in PyTorch, with face and mouth landmark extraction handled through an existing face-alignment library and forced phonetic alignment performed with an existing open-source aligner, rather than building either component from scratch. Table II outlines the planned dataset composition across the training, validation, and two held-out test conditions described in Section IV-E. Training is planned to run on a single consumer-grade GPU, consistent with the project's aim of keeping the resulting method lightweight and reproducible without specialized infrastructure. As a baseline for comparison, the retrained classifier's accuracy on the era-matched 2019–2020 test condition is checked against the accuracy figures reported in the original study, providing a sanity check that the retraining procedure has not introduced a regression before the harder 2024–2026 condition is evaluated.

Two outcomes are possible, and each carries a different implication. If the retrained classifier maintains comparable accuracy against both held-out speakers and modern generation methods, the result would support the claim that mouth-closure phoneme mismatch is a durable, generator-independent property of synthetic speech, reinforcing the case for using this kind of lightweight, explainable cue in production moderation and verification pipelines rather than resource-heavy black-box classifiers. If accuracy instead degrades noticeably against the newer generation methods, that would indicate the cue itself — not just the classifier trained on it — needs to be supplemented, most plausibly by combining it with the identity-dynamics or temporal-consistency signals used in more recent multimodal work such as PIA [3], rather than by further retraining alone.

Either outcome is useful to the field. A negative result narrows down exactly which property of modern synthesis — improved temporal smoothness, better viseme approximation, or something else — has closed the gap the original technique exploited, which is itself informative for anyone designing the next generation of cue-based detectors. The main limitation of the planned study is that it evaluates against a necessarily incomplete sample of current generation methods; deepfake generation is a fast-moving target, and conclusions drawn from methods available in 2026 may not hold against tools released even a year later. A second limitation is that forced phonetic alignment is itself imperfect, and residual alignment error could be mistaken for a genuine phoneme-viseme mismatch, which is why a manually verified subset is retained as a check on the automatic labeling pipeline.

This project retrains and re-evaluates a well-known lip-sync deepfake detection cue — phoneme-viseme mismatch during bilabial sounds — under two conditions the original study never tested: multiple speakers and modern deepfake generation methods. The outcome will clarify whether this lightweight, interpretable forensic technique continues to hold at scale, a question that matters directly for its practical use in content moderation, journalism, and legal evidence review. Future work beyond the scope of this capstone project could extend the retrained classifier with the identity-dynamics and audio-visual temporal cues used in recent multimodal detectors, evaluate robustness against real-time video-call deepfakes rather than pre-rendered clips, and test the cue's performance under common compression and re-encoding conditions found on social media platforms, since detection accuracy measured on lossless research video does not always survive the compression pipelines through which deepfakes are actually distributed.
